question: A patient who has eaten very little for 10 days is restarted on enteral feeding. On day 2 of feeding, he develops muscle weakness, cardiac arrhythmia, and his blood results show a falling serum phosphate. What is the most likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aspiration presents with respiratory symptoms (cough, fever, desaturation) — not the triad of muscle weakness, arrhythmia, and hypophosphataemia.

Correct. Refeeding syndrome occurs when carbohydrate reintroduction triggers a massive insulin-driven shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells. Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark; it causes muscle weakness (including respiratory muscles), arrhythmias, and cardiac failure.

answers.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state from excess carbohydrate loading

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state causes hyperglycaemia, dehydration, and altered consciousness — not the electrolyte shift pattern seen here.
C. difficile causes profuse watery diarrhoea and abdominal pain — not the cardiovascular and electrolyte picture described.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recognise refeeding syndrome by the setting (prolonged starvation, then refeeding) and the electrolyte pattern (hypophosphataemia is the hallmark). Prevention: check and correct phosphate/potassium/magnesium before starting feeds; begin feeds slowly at 50% of target.

Correct. Refeeding syndrome: falling phosphate + potassium + magnesium on restarting feeds in a starved patient, causing cardiac arrhythmia, muscle weakness, and respiratory failure. Prevention: correct electrolytes BEFORE feeding; start feeds at 50% of target rate.
